title: The Histories
author: Herodotus
openingText: Herodotus of Halicarnassus here presents his research so that human events do not fade with time, and that the great and marvellous deeds displayed by both Greeks and barbarians should not lack renown — and especially to show why they went to war with each other.
about: Herodotus set out to explain how Greece and Persia went to war. Along the way he interviewed everyone he could find, recorded every digression, and invented the discipline of history. Half of it is true. All of it is fascinating.

angleCards.title: Herodotus as the world's first journalist.
angleCards.text: He interviewed sources, weighed conflicting accounts, and regularly noted when he found something implausible but chose to report it anyway. I want to read tracking his method as much as his content.
angleCards.angleObjective: I'm reading Herodotus as the world's first journalist — tracking how he gathered information, when he signals doubt about his sources, and what his methods reveal about what ancient history actually is.

angleCards.title: Greece versus Persia as a civilisational argument.
angleCards.text: Herodotus isn't just narrating battles — he's arguing that freedom and tyranny produce different kinds of soldiers, different kinds of courage. I want to follow that argument through the whole work.
angleCards.angleObjective: I'm reading The Histories to understand the Persian Wars as a clash of civilisations — what Herodotus thinks the real difference between Greece and Persia is, and whether his analysis still holds.

angleCards.title: The digressions as the real point.
angleCards.text: Herodotus spends more time on Egypt, Scythia, and Babylon than on many of the battles. I want to read these digressions as a coherent project — an attempt to understand the whole world, not just one conflict.
angleCards.angleObjective: I'm reading The Histories for the digressions — Egypt, Scythia, Babylon, Libya — which I suspect are the real point of the work, and I want to understand what Herodotus was doing when he kept stopping to explore everything that wasn't the war.

angleCards.title: What Herodotus actually believed.
angleCards.text: He reports flying snakes, gold-digging ants, and rivers of amber — but often with explicit caveats. I want to track his sceptical markers and form a view of what kind of historian he was and what he thought he was doing.
angleCards.angleObjective: I'm reading The Histories asking whether Herodotus believed everything he wrote — I want to track the moments where he signals scepticism and understand what kind of historian he was trying to be.

cast.name: Herodotus
cast.description: Everywhere and nowhere — present in every digression and editorial comment, absent as a character. The voice that gathered, weighed, and arranged everything. Understanding his personality is most of the pleasure of the book.

cast.name: Croesus
cast.description: King of Lydia, the richest man in the world, who asked the oracle whether he should attack Persia and misread the answer. His story opens the whole work — a meditation on hubris, fortune, and the limits of human knowledge.

cast.name: Cyrus
cast.description: The first and greatest Persian king — conqueror of Lydia, Babylon, and most of the known world. His rise occupies Book 1. His death is a consequence of the same overreach that destroyed Croesus.

cast.name: Xerxes
cast.description: Led the largest army in ancient history against Greece. Herodotus gives him both grandeur and foolishness — weeping at the sight of his forces, then whipping the sea for destroying his bridge. The work's central antagonist.

cast.name: Themistocles
cast.description: The architect of the Greek victory at Salamis — who read the Oracle correctly, persuaded Athens to build a fleet, and then lured the Persian navy into a fight it couldn't win. Brilliant and unscrupulous in equal measure.

cast.name: Leonidas
cast.description: The Spartan king who held the pass at Thermopylae with 300 Spartans and died there. Herodotus knew the battle failed to stop Xerxes. He tells it anyway, at length, because he understood what the story meant.
